lessons.title: la herramienta — the tool
lessons.gloss: the tool — a thing of iron, with the iron still in the word

segments.source: [PAUSE 2s]

segments.text: Say el taladro and arreglar. The drill is one of these; name the category it belongs to.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: la herramienta

segments.text: la herramienta — the tool.
Una caja de herramientas — a toolbox. No tengo las herramientas — I haven't got the tools. La herramienta adecuada — the right tool for the job.
It covers the abstract sense as well: una herramienta muy útil about an app or a method, exactly as English uses "tool".

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the h that hides a diphthong

segments.text: Say it: e-rra-MIEN-ta. The h is silent, as it is anywhere in Spanish that it stands alone, and underneath it is the ie you have met before:

One rule governs both vowels, and it is the one you already have: a stressed e breaks, an unstressed one stays flat. In ferrum the stress is on the e, so it breaks — hierro. In ferramenta the stress has moved onto the suffix, so the first e stays flat — herra- — and the break happens where the stress went instead: -mienta, the very same -miento you have in el seguimiento.

The h is written because it was once spoken. Latin f- weakened to a breathy h in Castilian mouths, the breath faded, and the spelling stayed behind. That f-to-h shift is one of the loudest things Spanish did to Latin.
Latin ferramenta, "things made of iron" — the plural of ferramentum, from ferrum, iron.

So a herramienta is an iron thing, and the name is older than any of the tools you own. The same ferrum is the Fe on the periodic table, and it gives Spanish el hierro, el herrero — the blacksmith — and la herradura, a horseshoe.

That f to h is the signature of Spanish among the Romance languages. Latin facere gave hacer, filius gave hijo, ferrum gave hierro — while Italian kept ferro and French kept fer. The letter is silent now, but it marks where an f used to be.

lessons.title: solicitar — the word the form uses
lessons.gloss: to apply for, to request — the formal verb on the form

segments.source: [PAUSE 2s]

segments.text: Say la cita and entregar. Both belong to the same morning at a counter.
solicitar — to apply for, to request, formally.
Para solicitar una plaza, entregue la ficha antes del día 20.

Solicitar una beca — to apply for a grant. Solicitar cita previa — to book an appointment in advance, the phrase on Spanish health-centre and town-hall pages; much of Latin America says sacar turno or agendar una cita for the same act.
La solicitud is the application itself, and the piece of paper it is written on.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: solicitar is not pedir

utterances: what you are doing: asking a person for a thing. the verb: pedir.
what you are doing: asking an institution, on a form. the verb: solicitar.

segments.text: Le pido un café al camarero. Solicito una beca al ministerio. Using solicitar with a friend would sound as though you had filled in a form to borrow their drill.
That is the whole difference and it is register, not meaning: solicitar is the bookish arrival, worn nowhere down, and it belongs to writing.
Latin sollicitare: sollus, whole, plus citare, to set in motion — so to stir something entirely, to shake it up.

The oldest sense is agitation, and Spanish keeps that branch too: estar solícito is to be attentive, and English solicitous means anxiously caring, while solicitude is worry. To apply for something is to set the machinery in motion on your behalf.
That citare is the one inside la cita — an appointment is a summoning — and English cite, excite, recite and incite are all the same setting-in-motion.

lessons.title: la espera — the wait
lessons.gloss: the wait — the noun of esperar, and the sign above the chairs

segments.source: [PAUSE 2s]

segments.text: Say esperar and el plazo. One is the doing, one is the window. The noun between them is next.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: la espera

segments.text: la espera — the wait.
Sala de espera.
La lista de espera — the waiting list. Una espera de dos horas — a two-hour wait. En espera de su respuesta — awaiting your reply, the closing line of a formal letter.
The verb you already have; this is the noun that goes on the door.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: a noun made by cutting, not by adding

segments.text: You have four noun-making suffixes — three that work on verbs, and -eza, which works on adjectives. This is a fifth move, and it is the opposite of all of them: take the ending off.

Cut -ar and put back a bare -a or -o. You already have one of these: la entrega arrived two chapters ago without being named as a pattern. These are the shortest nouns in the language and among the commonest. What you cannot predict is which vowel a given verb will take — la compra but el pago. Once you have the word, the ordinary -o/-a rule hands you the article as usual.
Set beside la solicitud: one verb swaps its ending for -ud, the other drops its ending and puts back a single vowel. Both are ordinary.
Latin sperare, from spes, hope — though already in Latin it leaned as much on looking forward to as on hoping, and a Roman could sperare bad news as readily as good.

That middle sense is the hinge. Esperar took over the work of Latin exspectare, to expect, and ended up covering all three English verbs you met when you learned it: espero el autobús is waiting, espero el pan is expecting, espero que sí is hoping. La espera names only the first of them.
You met the same root in la esperanza, hope, which is -anza on this verb. So la espera and la esperanza are one word twice: the plain wait, and the hope that grew out of it.
The e- at the front is Spanish's own, the same one that turned stare into estar and stroppiare into estropear.

lessons.title: (la herramienta, solicitar, la espera) — from cold
lessons.gloss: cold retrieval of the three, and the fifth way Spanish turns a verb into a noun

segments.source: [PAUSE 3s]

segments.text: Close the lessons before this one. Say all three: the tool, to apply for, the wait.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: five ways to a noun, now complete

utterances: how: -anza. example: la mudanza. gender: feminine.
how: -miento. example: el seguimiento. gender: masculine.
how: -eza. example: la limpieza. gender: feminine.
how: -ción. example: la instalación. gender: feminine.
how: cut the ending. example: la espera. gender: either.

segments.text: The first four hand you the article. The fifth does not — la espera, la compra, but el pago and el gasto. The ending is no help in guessing which vowel a given verb takes; once you have the word, the ordinary -o/-a rule gives you the article as usual.
Note what that costs: these are the shortest and commonest nouns in Spanish, and they are the ones the endings cannot help you with.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: two of the three were relatives

utterances: new word: la herramienta. what it was built on: ferrum, iron — and el hierro.
new word: solicitar. what it was built on: citare, inside la cita.
new word: la espera. what it was built on: esperar, and la esperanza beside it.

segments.text: La espera is the neat one: esperar and la esperanza arrived together with the verb itself, long ago, and the moving chapter showed you the -anza that builds the second from the first. This is the third member — the plain noun that sits between the verb and the abstract one.

lessons.title: (pedir prestada una herramienta) — read it, then do it yourself
lessons.gloss: the payoff — read a noticeboard offering a tool library, then ask for one

segments.source: [PAUSE 2s]

segments.text: Say la herramienta and solicitar. The notice below uses one for the things and one for the paperwork.
A notice in a neighbourhood centre. Read it, then answer.
PRÉSTAMO DE HERRAMIENTAS.
Taladros, escaleras y carritos. Dos días por vecino.
Para solicitar una herramienta, rellene la ficha en conserjería.
Hay lista de espera para el taladro grande.

segments.source: [PAUSE 3s]

segments.instruction: what you can borrow, and for how long
segments.source: [YOU SAY: what you can borrow, and for how long]

segments.instruction: what you have to do to ask for one
segments.source: [YOU SAY: what you have to do to ask for one]

segments.instruction: which item you may not get straight away
segments.source: [YOU SAY: which item you may not get straight away]

segments.text: Solicitar on a noticeboard and pedir at the counter are the same act in two registers. The notice says para solicitar una herramienta because it is describing a procedure; the neighbour who walks in says ¿me dejas el taladro? That pair is the whole of Spanish formality in one scene.

Hay lista de espera — bare, with no article at all. The firm rule is what hay refuses: never hay la lista, because hay introduces a thing's existence rather than pointing at one already known. Between hay lista and hay una lista both are correct, and the bare noun is what a notice board uses.
And por vecino — "per neighbour" — is por doing distribution, the same por that gave a cause on the roadworks sign. One preposition, several jobs, and the noun after it stays bare.

segments.source: [PAUSE 3s]

segments.text: Now your turn, out loud and then in writing. Four lines for a tool library: say what is lent and for how long, say how to apply, say there is a waiting list, and then ask a neighbour informally for the same thing.
Then check yourself: did the notice use solicitar and the neighbour pedir?
